name: Perl
summary: Learn Perl 5 variables, hashes, regular expressions, subroutines, and line-based input with small scripts.

prerequisites: Know how to save a plain text file.
Install a Perl 5 interpreter to run examples from a terminal with perl lesson.pl. The examples use core features.
metadata.miniProject: Build a report from status lines such as INFO 12. Read lines through a filehandle, validate each line with an anchored regex, add totals by status in a hash, and sort the report.

lessons.title: Scalars, strictness, and interpolation
lessons.explanation: A scalar holds a single value. Its variable name begins with a dollar sign. Use my to declare a lexical variable. strict and warnings help catch mistakes early. Enable say to print a value with a newline.

api.name: my
api.description: Declare a lexical variable in the current scope.

api.name: use strict
api.description: Enable checks including the requirement to declare ordinary lexical variables.

api.name: say
api.description: Print values followed by a newline after enabling the feature.

lessons.practice: Print a title and a numeric total after adding two reading lengths.
lessons.pitfall: A double-quoted string interpolates a variable. A single-quoted string keeps its name as literal text.

exercise.expected: Declare the data with my and use double quotes to print the result.
exercise.completion: Reading lengths 14 and 9 produce 23 pages in the report.

lessons.title: Arrays, hashes, and defined defaults
lessons.explanation: An array stores an ordered list. A hash associates keys with values. Use the scalar form to access one element, such as $counts{$word}. The defined-or operator uses a fallback when the left value is undef.

api.name: @items
api.description: Use the array as a collection.

api.name: $counts{$key}
api.description: Access one scalar value by hash key.
Use the right operand only when the left operand is undefined.

lessons.practice: Count tags in ("code", "notes", "code", "lab") and print them in sorted order.
lessons.pitfall: Use // when zero is a valid value. The || operator also chooses its fallback for false values such as zero.

exercise.expected: Store one frequency per distinct tag.
exercise.completion: The output reports code: 2, lab: 1, and notes: 1 in order.

lessons.title: Match a whole line and capture fields
lessons.explanation: The =~ operator matches a value against a pattern. Use the start and end anchors when every character must fit the pattern. Parentheses capture parts you want to extract after a successful match.

api.description: Apply a match to a specific value.

api.name: \A and \z
api.description: Anchor a match at the start and actual end of the string.
Read captured groups after a successful match.

lessons.practice: Parse an item name with lowercase letters followed by one space and a positive quantity. Reject trailing text.
lessons.pitfall: A match without both anchors can accept a substring of invalid input. Check the complete format when validating records.

exercise.expected: Print the name and quantity only for valid records.

lessons.title: Pass arguments and handle an empty list
lessons.explanation: A subroutine receives its arguments in @_. Give intermediate values local names. This average helper returns undef for empty input and a number for a nonempty list.

api.description: Access the subroutine arguments. In scalar context this gives the count.

api.name: return
api.description: End the subroutine and send a value to its caller.

lessons.practice: Write a helper that returns the maximum of a numeric list or undef when it is empty. Include negative inputs.
lessons.pitfall: The elements of @_ can alias caller variables. Copy arguments into lexical variables if you plan to modify them locally.

exercise.expected: Distinguish an empty list from a list whose maximum is zero or negative.
exercise.completion: The inputs (-5, -2, -7), (0), and () produce -2, 0, and no values.

lessons.title: Read and close a filehandle
lessons.explanation: Use three-argument open to specify the mode and input independently. A scalar reference lets this example read text in memory. Read each line through the lexical handle, remove its line ending with chomp, and close the handle when finished.

api.name: open HANDLE, MODE, INPUT
api.description: Open a file or scalar for a specified mode and check success.

api.name: <$input>
api.description: Read the next line from the lexical handle.

api.name: chomp
api.description: Remove the current input record separator if it is present at the end.

lessons.practice: Replace the in-memory stream with a file path supplied as an argument. Report missing files clearly and print nonempty lines.
lessons.pitfall: Check open before reading from the handle. Use the separate mode and filename arguments for external files.

exercise.expected: Open a user-selected file for reading and handle failure explicitly.
exercise.completion: A file containing two nonempty lines prints two records. A missing file reports an open error.
